subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is a pathogen?
options: A type of white blood cell
A microorganism that causes infectious disease
questions.explain: A pathogen is a microorganism (virus, bacterium, fungus or protist) that causes an infectious, communicable disease that can spread between organisms.

questions.q: Which of these would help reduce the spread of a communicable disease?
options: Increasing contact between infected and healthy people
Good hygiene, isolating infected people, and vaccination
questions.explain: Spread can be reduced by good hygiene (e.g. handwashing), destroying vectors, isolating infected individuals and vaccination. These break the chain of transmission.

questions.q: Measles is caused by a virus. How is it mainly spread?
options: By droplets from sneezes and coughs (inhalation)
questions.explain: Measles is spread by inhalation of droplets from an infected person's sneezes and coughs. It can be serious, so most young children are vaccinated against it.

questions.q: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) affects plants by:
options: Causing a mosaic discolouration pattern on leaves that reduces photosynthesis
questions.explain: TMV causes a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves. This reduces the amount of chlorophyll and photosynthesis, so the plant grows poorly.

questions.q: Salmonella food poisoning is caused by bacteria. What causes the symptoms such as fever and diarrhoea?
options: A lack of white blood cells
questions.explain: Salmonella bacteria produce toxins that cause fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against Salmonella to control it.

questions.q: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted disease. How can its spread be controlled?
options: It cannot be controlled at all
By using antibiotics and barrier contraception such as condoms
questions.explain: Gonorrhoea (a bacterial STD) can be treated with antibiotics, though some strains are now resistant. Using a barrier method such as a condom helps prevent its spread.

questions.q: Rose black spot is a plant disease caused by a fungus. How does it affect the plant?
options: Purple/black spots on leaves that then turn yellow and drop, reducing photosynthesis
questions.explain: Rose black spot (a fungus) causes purple or black spots on leaves; leaves then turn yellow and drop early. This reduces photosynthesis and growth. It spreads in water and can be treated with fungicides.

questions.q: Malaria is caused by a protist. How is it transmitted?
options: By a mosquito acting as a vector
questions.explain: Malaria is caused by a protist spread by the mosquito, which acts as a vector. It causes recurrent fevers and can be fatal. Spread is reduced by preventing mosquitoes breeding and using mosquito nets.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-specific human defence against pathogens?
options: The skin acting as a barrier and stomach acid killing pathogens
questions.explain: Non-specific defences include the skin (barrier), nose hairs and mucus, trachea and bronchi (mucus and cilia), and stomach acid. Antibodies and memory cells are part of the specific immune response.

questions.q: Which type of white blood cell produces antibodies?
questions.explain: Lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to the antigens on a pathogen, and antitoxins to counteract toxins. Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis).

questions.q: How does a phagocyte destroy a pathogen?
options: It divides to form memory cells
It engulfs and digests the pathogen
It produces antibodies that lock onto antigens
questions.explain: Phagocytes carry out phagocytosis: they engulf pathogens and digest them using enzymes. Lymphocytes deal with pathogens by producing antibodies and antitoxins.

questions.q: How does a vaccine make a person immune to a disease?
options: It injects antibiotics that kill the pathogen
It removes all pathogens from the body permanently
It introduces small quantities of dead or inactive pathogen so white blood cells produce antibodies and memory cells
It gives the person the full disease
questions.explain: A vaccine contains a small amount of dead or inactive pathogen. This stimulates lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory cells, so if the live pathogen invades later the response is faster and larger.

questions.q: What is meant by herd immunity?
options: Immunity that lasts only one day
Immunity gained without any white blood cells
If a large proportion of the population is vaccinated, the spread of the pathogen is greatly reduced
questions.explain: When a large enough proportion of a population is vaccinated, there are too few susceptible people for the pathogen to spread easily, protecting even unvaccinated individuals. This is herd immunity.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics NOT used to treat viral infections such as flu?
options: Antibiotics kill bacteria but cannot kill viruses inside body cells
questions.explain: Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, which reproduce inside the body's own cells. It is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the host tissue.

questions.q: Why is the emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (e.g. MRSA) a concern?
options: Resistant strains are not killed by antibiotics, so infections are harder to treat
questions.explain: Overuse and inappropriate use of antibiotics have led to resistant strains such as MRSA, which are not killed by common antibiotics. This makes infections harder to treat and spread rapidly.

questions.q: The heart drug digitalis originally came from which source?
questions.explain: Digitalis (a heart drug) was extracted from foxgloves. Aspirin originates from willow, and penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from Penicillium mould. Many drugs originate from plants and microorganisms.

questions.q: During clinical trials of a new drug, what is tested first in the preclinical stage?
options: Toxicity, efficacy and dose using cells, tissues and live animals
Efficacy and dose in a large group of patients
questions.explain: New drugs are first tested in preclinical trials on cells, tissues and live animals for toxicity, efficacy and dose. Clinical trials on healthy volunteers and then patients follow, often double-blind with a placebo.

questions.q: How are monoclonal antibodies produced? (Higher tier)
options: By fusing a mouse lymphocyte with a tumour cell to make a hybridoma that divides and makes identical antibodies
By extracting them from soil bacteria
questions.explain: A mouse is stimulated to make lymphocytes producing a specific antibody. These are fused with a tumour cell to form a hybridoma, which divides rapidly and produces large amounts of identical (monoclonal) antibodies.

questions.q: Which is a use of monoclonal antibodies?
options: Pregnancy tests, diagnosis, and targeting specific cells such as cancer cells
questions.explain: Monoclonal antibodies are used in pregnancy tests, measuring hormone/molecule levels, detecting pathogens, research, and targeting drugs to specific cells such as cancer cells. They caused more side effects than first hoped.

questions.q: Which is a physical defence response that plants use against pathogens?
options: A waxy cuticle and cellulose cell walls that act as barriers
questions.explain: Plant physical defences include a waxy cuticle, cellulose cell walls and layers of dead cells (e.g. bark). Chemical defences include antibacterial chemicals and poisons; mechanical defences include thorns and hairs.
